segments.text: Hello and welcome to The Health Report with me, Norman Swan. Today we'll get beyond the hype on medicinal cannabis, a follow-up on the rotten fish oil capsule debate, beating heart surgery, the question to ask your cardiac surgeon before she does your bypass grafts, and is testosterone the elixir of youth for men?
The latest in a series of trials of testosterone supplementation in older men has been reported, and if you or someone you know is thinking of testosterone, then need to listen to this.
The person who wrote the commentary that went with the papers is Australian researcher and
international authority on testosterone, Professor David Handelsman, who's director of the Anzac
Research Institute at Concord Hospital in Sydney. Welcome to The Health Report.
Pleasure.
Tell me about these studies that were published recently in the Journal of the American Medical
Association.
These studies go back about a decade. It's known that testosterone levels fall a bit,
variably, over men's ageing. And the question was whether if that was restored, whether
that would improve men's health in all sorts of ways, including sexual function, but other
functions as well. NIH funded seven studies out of a common core protocol with seven different
endpoints. So they recruited a bunch of men and you got thrown into different parts of the study.
People could participate in up between one and seven of the different studies,
all at the same time, depending on what was being observed as they were going through 12
months of treatment with either testosterone or placebo. So that's a high quality randomized
control trial. And these were men who didn't have abnormally low testosterone levels,
they didn't have what's called hypogonadism. They didn't have pathological disorders of
the reproductive system, which is the classic indication for using testosterone treatment.
These were men who had a reduction in testosterone for unknown reasons, but not due to reproductive
disorders. And that could be anything from being obese, for being unfit, for having cardiovascular
disease, being depressed. There are many, many conditions which lower your testosterone because
testosterone is really like a barometer of health. So the question was, if testosterone is lowered
for any reason, not disorders of the reproductive system, does replacing it make a difference? Does
it improve health? So some of the studies have reported beforehand and these were into thinking
ability. The ones that had reported last year were actually in sexual function, physical activity and
energy levels. And those showed that there was a transient short-term effect on improving sexual
function, but it wore off during the study. And there was no effect on vitality or on physical
activity. That was reported in 2016. You and I spoke about it then. Yes, indeed. And these studies
are the other four. So there were three endpoints reported in 2016. These four endpoints were
reported now in February. And essentially, they showed that very convincingly, a large proportion
of all the men in the combined studies were in the study looking at cognitive function, that is
thinking or ability to reason and so on. And that was a clear negative. It was overwhelmingly
negative. And I think it's going to say negative, there was no result. It didn't make it worse.
They didn't make it better, didn't make it worse. And it more or less settles the idea that
testosterone could make such an improvement. The two other studies that were reported that
showed side benefits, small increases in hemoglobin. So less likely to be anemic.
Less likely to be anemic, but the difference was smaller than the difference between men and women.
And there was also an improvement in bone density, but again, a very small effect.
But the real headline out of these studies was the cardiovascular endpoint, which was
looking at coronary artery plaque. That is the plaque, which is the reason why coronary arteries
get blocked or any arteries get blocked actually. And they were able to measure that and accurately
measure it for the first time. And they showed that over the 12 month period, the testosterone
actually made the plaques worse. It caused narrowing of the blood vessels, which is really
an ominous finding, never been reported with any drug before. Although they didn't look at hard,
at what are called hard endpoints.
So they didn't look at heart attacks and strokes?
It was only a 12-month study.
It wasn't able to look at the really long-term cardiovascular effects.
But this must be one of the most convincing things
for coronary artery disease, actually measuring the plaque itself.
So we're dealing with men who don't have what's called
pathologically low testosterone levels in these trials,
if you like, kind of ordinary men,
but they might be unhealthy for various reasons.
But there is this group of men who've got what's called hypogonadism
with pathologically low levels of testosterone.
Are these heart plaque findings from this study a worry for them?
I wouldn't use the term hypogonadism or pathologically low to refer to them.
These are men who don't have disorders of the reproductive system.
In that setting, I think it is a concern.
It's quite ominous in a way to show that there is increased coronary plaque.
And what about men with reproductive disorders
and that's the reason they've got low testosterone?
The likelihood is that they're protected from cardiovascular disease over the years when they have low testosterone.
Replacing it should really bring them back to normal.
Just take someone who's had both their testes removed.
It's a replacement.
You're simply restoring back to physiology what nature or disease has removed.
It's very different when someone has a functional disorder due to obesity, being smoking or cardiovascular disease that causes a low testosterone.
In those situations, testosterone is a concern,
but the right thing to do is to remove the cause of the low testosterone
because it's reversible.
So it comes back up?
Yes, it does.
And the best examples of that are in obesity,
where clearly testosterone recovery occurs proportional
to how much reduction in weight.
Going on a diet tomorrow.
And we've just recruited the thousandth patient
to the largest ever trial of testosterone in Australia.
It's one of the great coincidences that on the day
that these studies came out in JAMA,
the T4DM, testosterone for diabetes, Mellitus study, which was an Australian study under Gary
Wittett's guidance in Adelaide, recruited its thousandth participant. This study is already
substantially larger than the testosterone trials, which have just been the subject of what we've
been talking about, where they had less than 800 men studied for a year. The testosterone trials
are a thousand men for two years. So when they come out in about two years time, they will be
the biggest study ever done. And looking at diabetes prevention. Looking at prevention of
diabetes, quite remarkable because it's done in Australian efficient clinical research terms on
a tenth of the US budget. So is this the end of testosterone supplements for men? Well, for men
with pathological disorders, by no means is at the end. In fact, that just continues because it's a
natural and reasonable form of replacement therapy for something's missing. Whether testosterone can
be used for pharmacological purposes is a question that can always be addressed like it is in the T4DM
study with a proper placebo-controlled study. It just shouldn't be used on a wide scale without
prior information safety and efficacy. And at this point, I should say that the context is important
here because in the last 30 years, there's been a hundredfold increase in testosterone sales without
any proven new indications for it. And in the US and in Canada, over one decade from 2000 to 2011,
there was a 40-fold increase in Canada and a 10-fold increase in the US, all without any
justification medically. So it's not the end of testosterone. It's probably the end of frivolous
uses of testosterone, but proper uses as a powerful drug still has quite a future,
but it should be based on proper trials. David Handelsman, thanks for joining us.
Pleasure. Professor David Handelsman, who's director of the Anzac Research Institute at
the University of Sydney. And you're listening to The Health Report here on RN, ABC News Radio,
and CBC Radio across Canada. Now to a story that might prove handy one day.
When you have three or more blocked coronary arteries, or a blockage on what's called the left
main coronary artery, also called the widow's artery, and you don't need too much imagination
to wonder what that's about, then avoiding stents and going to open heart coronary artery bypass
surgery is usually the best option. Trouble is that this surgery is associated with a risk of
stroke. Some surgeons have blamed the heart bypass machine for this, or unnecessary manipulation of
the aorta which comes off the heart, which is why some surgeons try to do off-pump bypasses on the
beating heart. The question, and it's a big one, is whether it makes a difference, which is why an
international research group led by Australians has analysed the evidence. With me in the studio
is one of the senior authors, cardiothoracic surgeon Michael Vallely of Sydney and Macquarie
Universities. Welcome to the Health Report, Michael. Thank you, Norman, for having me. Let's just get the context right here
and the various procedures that are available, because it's largely an elderly group of people
you're talking about here who need this. That's not entirely correct, but yes, I mean,
obviously coronary artery disease can happen in people in their 20s, and I've certainly operated on people
up to their 90s, so it's a wide spectrum. But the average age, and that's been
consistent, is around the 67, 68-year-old mark, and certainly
that has been responsible for the, yeah, of course, the younger, it gets younger.
Of course you get to it, yeah.
Exactly.
And so I think the advances in cardiovascular medicine and cardiovascular surgery is the
reason that, one of the reasons the population is living so long now.
So we've done this story before in the Health Report a few years ago, where people say,
look, the pump's a dreadful thing.
It can break off all sorts of rubbish, which goes up into the brain, causing cognitive
difficulties and stroke.
And you've got to get people off the pump.
And so there was a lot of promotion of beating heart surgery in those days.
and then it went off the boil and people had gone back to the pump.
So what's the story here?
I think there's a couple of issues there.
One is it's a technically more difficult procedure to do
and certainly there were some issues with the technical aspects of that.
Because you've got a moving target.
Moving target and positioning of the heart and also choice of patients
and also training.
I think we've been fortunate and the surgery's been around
for more than 20 years now and there's a group of us
that are dedicated to doing that procedure.
I think the other thing too is that people thought it was the heart-lung machine
that was causing the trouble and not the aorta.
The aorta is the main artery or the main pipe
that comes out of the heart
that delivers blood to the rest of the body.
And as people age and as their comorbidities increase,
diabetes, cardiovascular disease, smoking, obesity, etc.,
you can get disease within the aorta.
And if bits of that disease break off
and goes elsewhere in the body,
particularly to the brain, that's how you have a stroke.
And so what we and certainly a group of surgeons
that taught me at North Shore
and other surgeons around the world
thought that it wasn't actually the heart-lung machine that caused the problem,
was actually manipulating the aorta.
And part of the heart-lung machine is to manipulate aorta,
putting cannulas to return the blood.
And how you stop the heart is by putting a big clamp across the aorta
to stop the heart to do open-heart surgery.
Very interesting.
And so we've got a procedure,
and the other researchers in this large meta-analysis have got a procedure
where you can completely avoid manipulating the aorta
and just perform the bypass grafts using inflow from other arteries.
And just to clear up any confusion,
there are procedures where you do operate on the beating heart,
but you still manipulate the aorta.
So it's not a guarantee that...
There's different degrees.
There's a term that was coined by one of my training surgeons,
John Breda North Shore, which is anaortic,
which is a term that we've used as a simpler version of aortic no-touch.
So essentially there's different degrees of aortic manipulation
from absolutely no aortic manipulation,
which is the procedure that we've highlighted
as the initial procedure within this network meta-analysis
which looks at four different ways of doing the surgery
to minimal aortic manipulation to a clamp manipulation
into a full-blown arrested heart and heart-lung machine
with a cross clamp.
So there's different degrees of aortic manipulation.
And so what endpoints were you looking at in the analysis?
Because you looked at basically the international literature
in this field.
The international literature, it's interesting.
The numbers look large, but in terms of the scale
of the procedure, they're quite small.
But what we looked at, the major endpoint
that we were interested in was stroke
and neurocognitive injury.
And the patients that had the procedure done
with the minimal aortic manipulation
had a much larger incidence of preoperative stroke
and preoperative neurological problems.
So they were at greater risk of stroke.
So at greater risk of stroke, but they had a drastic reduction in stroke.
So if you actually did a propensity score analysis between the groups,
the results would probably have been more impressive.
So just to clear, so the surgeons were pre-selecting patients
and saying, well, I better not touch the aorta
because they're going to have a stroke.
Yes, yes.
And then so they're particularly hard.
You're loading the dice against the results.
Loading the dice against the results.
But in fact, they had reduced levels of stroke.
Yes, that's correct.
And presumably that played out for people not at a particularly increased risk of stroke.
Yes, yes.
So let's just then clear the space here because you've got an army of interventional cardiologists
whose mortgages depend on them putting in stents.
You've got another army of cardiothoracic surgeons who also have mortgages.
I'm being facetious, but...
I think it's a very valid point, actually, Norman, yes.
so what when do you need bypass surgery and then what should you be asking your surgeon about
beating heart surgery if you need bypass surgery i think you come back even further i think one of
the issues is you need an institutional or a heart team approach to the management of patients with
cardiovascular disease so the patient has uh there's an agnostic view of what they need so
it's a team absolutely and it needs to be done in a team and certainly the european model i think
we're lagging a little bit behind in Australia, but in a separate type of disease, and so the
structural heart disease and transcatheter valves, we have heart teams that, and the patient gets
the correct procedure. But you're absolutely right. You've got different craft groups competing for
the same procedure. So what are the indications for a bypass in a team-based? The indications
is obviously patients with complex coronary artery disease, patients, as you very elegantly pointed
out at the introduction, with left main, with severe triple vessel disease, patients with poor
left ventricular function. Certainly patients with diabetes do poorly with stents. Patients
who may not be compliant with medication that's required to keep stents patent. And certainly
patients who need other types of heart surgery as well need bypass surgery on top of that.
So you don't want to have a stroke, but not every cardiac surgeon is trained to do beating
heart surgery. So what are the questions to ask? I think there's several things you should ask
your cardiac surgeries. One is how many of these have you done? Two, what are your results? And if
not, then who should I be going to? And I think that's a very valid question to ask any doctor,
not just your cardiac surgeon. Keep your hands off my aorta. Yes. Michael, thanks for joining us.
Thank you. It's been a pleasure. Professor Michael Vallely of Macquarie and Sydney Universities and
Sydney Heart and Lung Surgeons. A couple of weeks ago, we ran what has become one of our more
controversial stories for a wee while. And that's because so many of you are wolfing down fish oil
capsules every day. Two researchers, one from Harvard and the other from the University of
Auckland, reported analysing a variety of fish oil capsules and finding only a fraction of the
content were the advertised omega-3 fatty acids, with the rest often containing saturated fat.
Not a great idea if you're taking fish oil for your heart, perhaps. And then when they looked
at the omega-3 fatty acids, they were often oxidised. They were off. We poo-pooed an industry
sponsors study which found the opposite but received a detailed email from Professor Peter
McLennan of Wollongong University who reckons our story was wrong. Peter has researched fish oils
and the heart for decades and he's in our Wollongong studio as we speak. Welcome Peter.
Good evening Norman. So let's start out, well let's start out with on a bigger picture before
we get to fish oil capsules because I don't want to waste the opportunity of having you on the
program because of your experience in this area. Why did fish oil start off with great hope about
preventing sudden cardiac death and so on and so forth? And every time a new meta-analysis comes
out, the effect size of fish oil becomes less, such that you question whether it's worth taking
it at all, even if the stuff inside is good. Well, it really probably comes down to how
well, we understand fish oil is working, Norman.
The very first indications suggested that it may be working
by preventing thrombosis and clotting
because that is a well-known action
with very high doses of the omega-3 fatty acids.
And the other indication is in atherosclerosis
and coronary artery disease.
But as we've followed this research through the epidemiology,
we're finding that the main effect is not in preventing heart attacks,
preventing the atherosclerosis,
but indeed preventing that from causing fatal arrhythmias
and or preventing...
So sudden cardiac death.
Yes, sudden cardiac death.
But I thought even that had been disproven by the large trials
suggesting no, it doesn't even do that, even though there was hope of it.
No. Well, the trials that have examined sudden death in clearly defined communities that are at high risk of sudden death have come out in favour of it.
The GC Prevencioni trial in particular in Italy.
where we've run into problems is that you can't do sudden death studies in the general population
because we don't know who's going to have one and we just can't collect enough data.
So it's got to be in a naturalist group such as Michael Vallely's patients.
Such as people who have already had a previous heart attack are at very high risk of an arrhythmia that will kill them.
And so if we restrict the studies to those patients, then we'll see a protective effect.
What happens is that even those patients are hard to get in enough numbers.
So people have been combining patients who have had a stroke, patients who have had a myocardial infarction, patients who have had angina.
And expecting that they will see...
Two mixed to group.
Two mixed to group, yes.
But 45% of adults over 45 in New South Wales are taking fish oil.
They're not at risk of sudden death and they think it's doing something else for them.
It's a massive industry.
I would doubt that number because when we do the nutrition surveys,
the Australian National Survey of all sorts of nutrients,
nutrients, the indication is that intake of omega-3 fatty acids is very low across the population.
Right. I think it comes from the 45 and up study, but we can always check that later.
So then the question, so what you're saying is, and what about dose, sorry, even if you're taking
it for sudden death, are the doses high enough? Because that's been the argument, say, from the
group in Adelaide with arthritis, is that you've really got to take a lot of fish oil to get an
anti-inflammatory effect? That's correct. The anti-inflammatory effects do take high doses
and it is quite effective in that. So what's a high dose? Well, for arthritis, I think they're
using 10 milliliters or 10 grams a day, 10 capsules. So 10 capsules or 10 mils of liquid.
It's a very high dose. Also for lowering clinical hypertriglyceridemia, you need
four to six grams of the active omega-3 fatty acids to lower it. So that's again a therapeutic
effect. What we're talking about is protecting the heart through correcting a deficiency more than
having a drug-like effect. Okay so let's talk about the fish oil capsules and what's inside them.
A New Zealand study looking at Australian and New Zealand products, a Canadian study and a study at
Harvard all seem to show the same thing. A third of the content is omega-3 fatty acids. We need
to imagine it's all omega-3 fatty acids. The rest is significantly saturated fat. And then when they
look at the omega-3 fatty acids, it's oxidized. In other words, oxygen has got in and it's gone off.
But you don't agree with the findings of these three studies?
Well, for starters, the natural content of most fish oils is about 30%,
percent EPA plus DHA, which are the active components. And that's always been the case.
So that's not a surprise.
To find that there's only 30 percent of them in it is just to find that that's correct.
The other conflict was about the presence of saturated fat. Well, saturated fat is present
in the fish and in the fish oil at about the same level, about 30 percent. And indeed,
when we first started to investigate fish oil, we were looking at the difference between
polyunsaturates in general and saturated fatty acids. So at that time in the mid-80s,
saturated fat was the baddie. And we started using fish oil because it had less polyunsaturates
than the highly unsaturated vegetable oils. And we expected to get findings somewhere in between
the two, but in fact, the fish oil outperformed the sunflower seed oil and safflower oils
many fold. And we couldn't, if we diluted it with saturated fats, we didn't lose the effect.
So it overwhelmed the effect of whatever saturated fat was in there.
So what about the oxidation issue?
Yeah, the oxidation, I'm not an expert in the processes and the degree of oxidation
that are specified for safety reasons
are well under the potentially dangerous levels.
It's very difficult to actually oxidise fish oil.
In the body, it oxidises...
But David Cameron Smith reckoned it's very easy
when you look at the supply chain.
I think he has conducted a study
where he used oxidised fish oil
and had to bubble it with oxygen for 30 days or more
to get a significant degree of oxidation.
When we first started using fish oils,
we actually got it as a waste product from a safkol cannery in Melbourne
and it was like tar.
We didn't consider it satisfactory for human consumption.
It was being used for paints.
but it was very effective in preventing arrhythmias in our animal models.
So consumers can be reasonably relaxed, bottom line.
Absolutely.
Peter McLennan will have to leave it there.
Thank you very much for joining us.
You're welcome.
Peter McLennan from the Faculty of Science, Medicine and Health
at the University of Hoolam Gong.
You pay your money, you take your chance.
If you were to believe the general and sometimes business media coverage
about cannabis for medicinal purposes,
you could be for thinking it's a done deal,
works for all sorts of things and should be immediately put in the market.
Consumer groups add to this by pressing governments hard and there's strong public support.
Experts in cannabis, however, are a bit more circumspect,
and one of these is Professor Wayne Hall of the University of Queensland,
who even advised the British House of Lords on cannabis.
Wayne is in our Brisbane studio. Welcome to The Health Report, Wayne.
Thanks, Norman.
So, I mean, there really is broad public support for this, isn't there?
Yes, there has been in surveys probably for the better part of a decade.
And I think that's for understandable reasons,
when I think the general public would take the view
that if people have a serious and terminal illness in particular,
then there shouldn't be an eye access to a drug
that might ease their suffering.
So do people have a much broader sense of what it works for
than what it does actually work for?
I think they do.
There's a very recent review published
by the National Academy of Science in the US
which I think looked at some 20-odd indications
that cannabis has been prescribed for,
particularly in the US, allegedly for medicinal purposes.
And they found a very small list of indications
for which there was some evidence of effectiveness.
In the majority of cases,
their conclusion was that it was modestly effective
for some of these indications.
Such as?
Well, the best supported one is for treating nausea and vomiting
in cancer patients undergoing chemotherapy.
The evidence there is pretty old.
It was done and most of it was collected in the 1980s and the comparison was placebo or a drug that's no longer used.
We don't have good comparisons of cannabinoids or particularly THC tetrahydrocannabinol, the main ingredient in cannabis, is the one that appears to be therapeutic.
We don't have good studies, recent studies, comparing that to newer drugs which are very effective in treating nausea.
And when you're talking about medicinal cannabis, you're talking about an extract of cannabis plants, not just smoking raw cannabis.
Yes, we're talking either about a synthetic form of the active ingredients,
either the tetrahydrocannabinol or THC,
or more recently cannabidiol or CBD,
which has now been explored for therapeutic uses,
particularly in epilepsy,
and some standardized preparations such as the nabixamols
or drugs like Sativex,
which are combination standardized extracts from the cannabis plant.
So there's chronic pain as well,
which has been shown to be a bit effective for,
and in multiple sclerosis when you've got muscle spasticity.
It seems to work quite well for those.
Well, the muscle spasticity that patients report benefits,
but it's difficult to see objective signs of improvement in the trials.
So what's it used for in the United States?
Just about anything and everything,
particularly in places like California
where they've got a system that really doesn't deserve
to be taken seriously as a form of medicinal cannabis
because they're the average age of people in the medicinal cannabis programs is about 35.
They're male.
They've been using daily since their mid-teens.
And they don't have cancer.
They don't have AIDS.
They don't have neurological diseases.
So they're swallowing medicinal instead of smoking dope.
Well, yes.
And I think that's the complication, particularly in the US,
that medicinal cannabis has been used in some states as a sort of Trojan horse
for legalisation of recreational use.
So what's it going to look like in a strip?
Well, I think the governments, the federal and state governments here have very sensibly decided to approve,
well, look to approving the use of medicinal preparations,
either drugs like THC or CBD or standardised cannabis extracts,
if they prove to be effective in clinical trials.
And the clinical trials we're doing are what?
In the area of intractable epilepsy in childhood,
in treatment of nausea and vomiting in cancer patients
and also as a treatment palliative care
in easing the suffering of people with terminal forms of cancer.
And HIV AIDS, which has been popular here?
In the past, the issue with HIV AIDS is that people don't get AIDS.
That is the full clinical syndrome anymore
because the highly effective antiretroviral drugs people don't get to that state.
So the need for that use has really declined.
And the evidence there, certainly the National Academy of Science Review
concluded that the evidence was very weak, that it was effective for that use.
So there's going to be some disappointed members of the public
when a rather limited set of indications comes out.
I think that's likely to be the case.
And I think it's important that people have more realistic expectations
about what it might deliver.
I think the indication that's showing most promise at the moment
is intractable epilepsy. There's been a number of trials in the US. We haven't seen the published
versions, but reports at conferences suggest around about a third of children with rare forms
of intractable epilepsy have responded positively to the drug. And given the lack of treatment for
some of these conditions, that's an outcome that's to be welcomed.
Well, we'll watch this space closely and probably have you back. Wayne, thanks for joining us.
You're welcome.
Wayne Hall from the Centre of Youth Substance Abuse Research
and the Queensland Centre for Mental Health Research
in the School of Public Health at the University of Queensland.
I'm Norman Swan. This has been The Health Report.
Do join us next week.
